title: Report on Adult Safeguarding
dek: The Department of Health has not finished drafting the general scheme of the proposed safeguarding Bill. Continued inaction will inevitably expose more adults to the risk of abuse and neglect.

Cathaoirleach’s Foreword
Despite longstanding calls for the introduction of safeguarding legislation, successive governments have been far too slow to act – notwithstanding a series of high-profile abuse scandals.
In July 2025, the Joint Committee on Health considered the legal and policy gaps in adult safeguarding with Safeguarding Ireland and the Irish Association of Social Workers.
Almost a year on from that meeting, the Committee is deeply concerned that the necessary legislation has still not been published.

It is now nine years since Senator Colette Kelleher introduced a Private Members Bill on adult safeguarding. Despite cross-party support for the Bill, and the indisputable and urgent need for legislation, we are still waiting for meaningful reform.
Furthermore, two years on from the Law Reform Commission’s comprehensive report
A
Regulatory Framework for Adult Safeguarding,
which included draft legislation, the
Department of Health has still not finished drafting the General Scheme of a Safeguarding Bill – despite being on this Government’s legislative programme since Spring 2025.
This delay cannot be accepted any longer. Continued inaction will inevitably expose more adults to the risk of abuse and neglect.
Too many adults have already fallen through the cracks in our current systems. This is because these systems are totally inadequate to safeguard them.
This must urgently change.
A country with such a long and dark history of abuse should know better and do better.
Pádraig Rice TD
Cathaoirleach of the Joint Committee on Health
Rapporteur’s Introduction
There is an urgent need for the Oireachtas to act against adult abuse across every sector of society.

Whether we are concerned with Áras Attracta, Leas Cross, the care of loved ones at home or in care homes, with the treatment of Grace, or the indefensible failures in the Brandon case, adult safeguarding legislation is a concern for us all.

This was most recently highlighted by an RTÉ Investigates programme into two residential care facilities in 2025, but we are constantly reminded by HIQA reports, news, and community experiences of the need for robust adult safeguarding laws.
Adult Safeguarding legislation was first introduced by Senator Colette Kelleher in March 2017, sparking a legislative debate which continues 9 years later.
The Law Reform Commission published a comprehensive report in April 2024, complete with draft legislation.
The Commission’s engagements and considerations were extensive and deep. Notably, the
Commission recommends a statutory Inter-departmental Implementation Group and Sectoral Implementation Plans.
In April 2024, the Joint Committee on Disability Matters published its report
Ensuring rights based adult safeguarding in Ireland,
endorsing a national safeguarding authority and an integrated, cross-sectoral approach.

Various organisations and people have contributed to the movement for action and are understandably frustrated that adult safeguarding has been a focus of conversation, but not action, for the last decade.
There is a stark contrast in the sectoral approach of the Department of Health published at the end of December 2025 and the whole-of-government approach advocated strongly by most stakeholders.

The intention of this report is not to re-examine all the issues examined by previous reports. This report makes recommendations on the key issues of mandatory reporting, powers of access, oversight and accountability, independence, cross-sectoral cooperation, and independent advocacy. The recommendations touch on some ancillary matters.
The attention of the Government and the Oireachtas was drawn to the need for legislative provision for the protection of adults who are at risk or vulnerable by a Law Reform
Commission report on the legal aspects of professional home care in 2011.
It was not until December 2025 that the Government produced legislation providing for basic regulation of home care providers. It cannot take that long for us to see real adult safeguarding laws.
David Cullinane, TD
Rapporteur
Recommendations
Recommendations for the Minister for Health and the Department of Health

The Minister for Health, in cooperation with the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration should introduce legislation to provide for the criminal offences of coercion, endangerment, abuse, neglect, ill-treatment, exposure to risk of serious harm or abuse, coercive control, and coercive exploitation, in line with definitions provided by the Law Reform Commission.

The Minister for Health, in cooperation with the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Minister for Children, Disability, and Equality should bring forward adult safeguarding legislation to provide a statutory basis for the protection of adults at risk of harm, in line with definitions provided by the Law Reform Commission.
Adult safeguarding legislation should create a whole-of-Government framework for preventing and responding to serious harm, abuse, neglect, coercion, and fraud concerning at-risk adults.

Adult safeguarding legislation should provide for an independent cross-sectoral safeguarding body and transitional sectoral bodies. A transitional sectoral body should be established urgently for the health sector.
Adult safeguarding legislation should provide for mandatory reporting of safeguarding concerns in defined professional contexts.

Safeguarding legislation should provide strong supports for patients and patient advocates and introduce complaints mechanisms concerning decisions made by non-clinical staff which affect a patient’s welfare.

Individual, professional, service, and system-level responsibilities must be clearly identified with appropriate training and assurances required by law. Accountability should be at the appropriate level, with proportionate sanctions. Complex legal or corporate arrangements should not be a barrier to transparency and accountability.
The initial responsibility should be on service providers to resource, support, and ensure standards in recruitment and service delivery.

An escalation pathway to an independent safeguarding body must be accessible for all complaints of a criminal nature and for other safeguarding concerns which are not appropriately addressed by the service provider in the first instance. The ambition must be for independent oversight of both State and non-State providers.
The Office of the Confidential Recipient should remain independent and should be enhanced.

Where inspectors of safeguarding or regulatory authorities find serious and/or sustained breaches, or circumstances of reckless endangerment or harm, they should be empowered to issue fixed penalties against responsible institutions, organisations, or persons.
Safeguarding bodies, in cooperation with other agencies as appropriate, must have warrantless power of access to all relevant places, including residential care facilities but not private homes.

With regard to safeguarding concerns in private homes, legislation should provide for summary power of access for An Garda Síochána to at-risk adults in cases of immediate concern, and otherwise for Court-sanctioned health assessments for the safeguarding body, as recommended by the Law Reform Commission.

Individuals should retain the right to reject intervention, and capacity should be presumed in respect of any question of the matter unless the contrary is shown in accordance with the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015.
There must be robust monitoring for compliance, and systems of assurance and inspection. The purpose of auditing should be to improve standards.
Health and care facility visitation rights and family rights to access records should be addressed in primary legislation.

In addition to adult safeguarding legislation, holistic health and social care law reform is needed. A comprehensive statutory framework is needed for social care across home, transitional, and residential care. A wider social care strategy is needed with regards to community engagement, aging, and integration.

Existing professional regulation must be updated to strengthen safeguarding protections, and currently unregulated and under-regulated professions should be brought within the remit of a professional authority.
Safeguarding should be given prominence in health sector education and training.
Recommendations for the Health Service Executive
The HSE is, in the main, a service provider, and should be regarded as such. The HSE should retain responsibility in the first instance for the services which it provides directly and indirectly.
Internal HSE safeguarding investigations should be conducted by teams under the Chief Social Worker.
Safeguarding practices should be standardised, and resources balanced across regions.
Safeguarding staffing should be exempt from Pay and Numbers Strategy restrictions.

The HSE should ultimately be subject to escalation to an independent safeguarding authority. In the interim, a transitional sectoral body should urgently be empowered with statutory responsibility for the health sector. This could involve a reorganisation of the Chief Social Worker and Safeguarding Teams, but it must be independent of the HSE.
As should be the case for any service provider, non-clinical decision-makers should be subject to statutory safeguarding obligations where managerial or organisational issues are concerned.
Overview of the Committees’ Consideration
In June 2025, the Committee on Health appointed David Cullinane, TD, to act as rapporteur on the matter of adult safeguarding.
In July 2025, the Committee on Health held a meeting in Public Session to consider the matter of legal and policy gaps in adult safeguarding. The Committee invited the following witnesses:
Safeguarding Ireland
Ms Patricia Rickard-Clarke, chairperson
Ms Annmarie O'Connor, programme manager
Mr. Mervyn Taylor, member of the board
Irish Association of Social Workers
Ms Caroline Walker Strong, chief operations officer
Mr. Liam Keogh, principal social worker
Dr. Sarah Donnelly, associate professor of social work in UCD.
Additional consultations were held in 2025 by the rapporteur with representatives of the Law Reform Commission, the Health Information and Quality Authority, and the Health Service Executive.
The Department of Health published a National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care Sector in December 2025.
As a related matter, Mr Mike Nesbitt,

Minister of Health in the Northern Ireland Executive, introduced the Adult Protection Bill in June 2025, and it is progressing through the Assembly’s parliamentary process. These developments have been noted in forming the recommendations for this report.
The Law Reform Commission published its extensive and comprehensive final report on this matter in April 2024.

Previously, in February 2021, the Committee on Health held a meeting in Public Session to consider the matter of a regulatory framework for adult safeguarding with the Law Reform Commission with the following witnesses attending:
Ms Justice Mary Laffoy, president
Dr. Andrea Mulligan, commissioner
Mr. Raymond Byrne, commissioner
Ms Rebecca Coen, director of research
Ms Leanne Caulfield, principal researcher.
In addition, the Committee has considered the matter during other engagements in relation to home
and residential care
, as have the Committee on Disability Matters
and the
Committee on Assisted Dying.
The Committee also notes contributions such as Safeguarding Ireland’s 2022 report
Identifying Risks and Responsibilities – The Case for a Comprehensive Approach to Safeguarding Vulnerable Adults
Summary of Findings
Reporting Requirements
There is a legislative void when it comes to adult safeguarding in Ireland, which creates opportunities for individuals to conduct abuse or harm on adults.

There are no statutory reporting duties of safeguarding concerns or incidents relating to adults. This stands in stark contrast to existing laws for child protection. This affects public and private care, at home and in care facilities.

There are prominent cases of serial abuse being hidden by directors, managers, and workers in private and public facilities which have passed without accountability due to a lack of statutory responsibilities covering adult safeguarding incidents. Similar cases of abuse have been documented in private homes which have highlighted significant systemic legal failings.

‘Abuse’ can take place in many different forms, including sexual or physical assault, financial abuse, and abuse in residential care settings. Abuse occurs when an individual’s well-being is overlooked, their choice and autonomy is limited, and their rights are ignored.

There is a persistent failure to report the abuse and neglect of vulnerable adults in Ireland. Research by the Department of Health shows that people do not know how or where to report abuse to indicating that there is no clear pathway for reporting abuse in Ireland.

This is because there is no adult safeguarding legislation which should define the legal parameters for reporting abuse. There is also no standalone adult safeguarding authority which should oversee reports of abuse.

Safeguarding incidents can arise through direct and indirect responsibility, can be caused by anyone from care workers to managers to family carers, can vary in significance and intensity, can occur anywhere from a dwelling, a care facility, or any third place, and invariably can and do occur outside of the health sector with varying crossover.
Navigating the differences between who, how, and where requires clear
and distinct law covering a variety of complex legal situations. This legal framework must vindicate personal liberties and navigate constitutional protections afforded to private dwellings.

Organisations and professionals who oversee adult safeguarding encounter adult abuse regularly. They are compelled to respond and to refer their cases on, but there is no clear pathway for reporting abuse. Even if abuse is reported, there is no followup mechanism to ensure that referrals are acted on. That is why we need a standalone adult safeguarding authority. Without it, the underreporting of abuse in Ireland will persist and the negative culture around reporting abuse will continue. Safeguarding Ireland, and many other stakeholders and professionals in this area, strongly recommend that an independent safeguarding authority receives and responds to reports of abuse.
The fact that there is no clear pathway for reporting abuse in Ireland means that there is a significant absence of timely reporting.

Without timely reporting and independent inspection, adults are put at further risk of harm as seen in the Brandon, Emily, and Grace cases. Those who encounter abuse are sometimes afraid to report it for fear of the consequences. We must raise awareness through education and training about the importance of reporting adult abuse and signpost the necessary steps for reporting. By raising awareness, it is hoped that a cultural shift will take place, whereby individuals are no longer afraid to report safeguarding issues.

The underreporting of abuse in Ireland has led to a lack of comprehensive data on adult safeguarding. Without a reliable reporting system, we have no data on the number of actual cases of abuse or on the number of referrals. This hampers our ability to deal with adult safeguarding effectively.

The Irish Association of Social Workers recommends the introduction of mandatory reporting in certain circumstances. Mandatory reporting would require people to report concerns of actual or suspected abuse. It could relate to a specific harm or serious harm and would apply to certain professionals who are involved in adult safeguarding. The introduction of mandatory reporting should be modelled on the

system in place under the Children First Act 2015. In Ireland, we have a two-tier system where employees are mandated to report child protection concerns, but not adult protection concerns. This suggests that adult abuse is somehow less serious, which needs to be rectified.

Mandatory reporting needs to be aligned with the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 and the adult who is at risk must be at the centre of all activities. It should apply where issues of coercive control, a lack of capacity or risk to others occur.
The Law Reform Commission’s Report:
A Regulatory Framework for Adult Safeguarding 2024

recommends that a suitably defined threshold of harm is necessary for the purposes of mandated reporting. The report termed it ‘reportable harm’ which should refer to: assault, ill-treatment or neglect in a manner that affects or seriously affects health, safety or welfare; sexual abuse; or serious loss of, or damage to, property by theft, fraud, deception or coercive exploitation.

The Commission recommends that reporting for certain professions and instances should be deemed mandatory, that particular criminal offences should be created, and recommends a balanced enforcement approach which has due regard to consent from the individual concerned and private dwelling protections.

Safeguarding is a responsibility of everybody. All relevant jobs should require competency in adult safeguarding and reporting procedures. Currently, staff are working in patient-facing roles, and even in safeguarding roles, with a lack of knowledge and expertise in reporting procedures.
Powers of Access

The current system of adult safeguarding in Ireland is unsustainable. The existing legislative framework falls short in terms of the settings to which it applies, the types of abuse involved, and the overall legislative basis.

While there is a fledgling structure for safeguarding issues in the HSE Safeguarding Teams, there is a lack of legal powers of access and protection which create complications where safeguarding incidents occur outside of HSE settings. The HSE’s Safeguarding and Protection teams have no statutory power to enter public or private dwellings, and a very limited policy basis for certain public facilities.

The Chief Inspector of Social Services (generally understood as HIQA, although legally distinct) has limited inspection powers related to certain private care facilities. The Chief Inspector does not handle individual clinical concerns as its remit is to act as a systems regulator.

In contrast to Ireland, equivalent bodies in Scotland, Wales, Canada, and Australia have expansive powers of access. A range of stakeholders have voiced the need for expanded powers of access in Ireland. These powers must allow authorities to gain access to individuals who would otherwise be invisible in the care system.

In the UK, the Care Act 2014 enshrines the rights of people who need care and support. We need similar legislation in Ireland to enshrine the rights of people with care needs. Too often, individuals recognise risks to adults but cannot implement a safety plan as they have no powers.

The Law Reform Commission recommends providing “authorised officers of the Safeguarding Body with a warrantless power of entry to and inspection of a relevant premises,” which is to be broadly defined but excluding private dwellings. Private dwellings in this case should exclude rooms in care facilities due to the broad range of access to such rooms.

Powers of entry should be used in a proportionate, appropriate, and consistent manner. This should be set out in legislation whereby powers of entry are warranted only in specified circumstances, where there is a reasonable concern, supported by evidence.
The conditions of exercising such powers should not, however, be so onerous as to discourage use of those powers.

The Law Reform Commission recommends that adult safeguarding legislation should permit a “safeguarding body” to: use powers of entry and inspection; apply for a warrant to access an at-risk adult’s premises; apply for a removal and transfer order for an at-risk adult; apply for an order under the Domestic Violence Act 2018 or an adult-safeguarding no-contact order for the at-risk adult; and assist members of An Garda Síochána in their summary power of access to an at-risk adult. Each of these powers should be carried out to assess and protect the health, safety and welfare of an at-risk adult.

The Law Reform Commission recommends safeguards for the use of summary powers of access, including recording its usage and notifying the safeguarding authority of its usage in a timely manner. Additional safeguards, such as ensuring the anonymity of the at-risk adult in court proceedings and an explanation of the warrant or power to be provided would be useful.
Legal powers of access and intervention should be vested in an independent safeguarding authority with a clear mandate for exercising such powers.
Oversight and Accountability

New legislation should target specific areas of adult safeguarding, including powers of access and protection. Legislation should function as a deterrent to be able to protect the at-risk adult and prosecute the alleged perpetrator if that is the individual’s preference.

The lack of oversight and accountability when it comes to adult safeguarding boils down to the fact that there is no single adult safeguarding authority in Ireland. Getting support with a concern about abuse requires navigating a complex system, where no single body is responsible or has the ability, expertise or resources to resolve the issues at hand.
The creation of an independent statutory adult safeguarding authority is necessary to ensure effective oversight and accountability. The authority must be tasked with

receiving reports of actual or suspected abuse, responding to reports, directing cases to the HSE and other statutory and non-statutory bodies, coordinating and conducting serious incident reviews, setting standards and monitoring compliance, developing safeguarding plans, putting in place preventative measures, conducting training, research and education programmes and overseeing data collection.

The new authority should be responsible for receiving and investigating individual complaints across the sector and overseeing the investigation of complaints, including where a person is not in receipt of any care services, as well as oversight of critical incidents.

It should be the role of the safeguarding authority and sectoral authorities to ensure standards of training across every sector. Effective training and awareness programmes should foster a culture whereby oversight and accountability in safeguarding cases are essential. The importance of individual accountability also needs to be taught.

To ensure oversight and accountability, there needs to be sufficient staff in each of the sectors. The Irish Dementia Working Group called for safe staffing levels, particularly in care settings. HIQA has an important role to play in ensuring that there are sufficient levels of staff in care settings. It should carry out inspections on systems of adult safeguarding as a form of quality control and a source of learning.

Oversight by regulatory bodies has been shown as less than always fully effective. There is a need for improvements in leadership, management, training and governance to promote positive cultural changes within organisations as well.

The Law Reform Commission recommends the creation of a regulatory framework that would include the assignment of responsibility for oversight and regulation to appropriate bodies. It also recommends that an interdepartmental steering group
should be established on a statutory basis in Ireland to provide oversight of cooperation in the adult safeguarding context.
Independence

There is a clear and strong case for an independent, wide-ranging safeguarding authority which is well evidenced in reports published by the Law Reform Commission and Safeguarding Ireland. Safeguarding bodies should be entirely independent of the services they are investigating.

Safeguarding policies and practices are developed to different levels across different sectors, and there is a need to develop and integrate cross-sectoral safeguarding services before a single body could be responsible for safeguarding investigations.

In the interim, independent transitional sectoral safeguarding bodies could be established. The Chief Social Worker and existing HSE safeguarding infrastructure could serve as the foundation for a transitional authority but will require real statutory powers to be effective.

The independent safeguarding body recommended by the Law Reform Commission could take the form of a statutory office, a unitary corporate entity, or a Board-like structure such as the model in the Adult Protection Bill being considered by the Legislative Assembly of Northern Ireland which would integrate sectoral safeguarding bodies into a single national framework. This question warrants further exploration based on practical considerations but should not be a cause of delay in enacting new legislation. The correct model is that which delivers prompt and effective action.
Cross-sectoral Cooperation

Safeguarding has often been viewed as a ‘Health and Social Care issue.’ However, it is much broader than that. It requires an inter-agency and cross-sectoral response, as well as a whole-of-society approach, enshrined with deep expertise.

There are serious legal and policy gaps in adult safeguarding, which extend beyond the Health and Social Care system into areas such as financial abuse, physical abuse, neglect, and the deprivation of liberty. From a legal perspective, it is also crosssectional, bringing in several areas of law, such as criminal, tort, banking, and family
law.

A key enabler of adult abuse is the lack of interagency cooperation and shared expertise. Data sharing and cooperation across agencies should be mandatory and professionals must be required to deepen their expertise and broaden their response. There is a lack of mandatory cooperation between actors and robust pathways for reporting concerns.

Several organisations and sectors play a role in adult safeguarding and each of them has relevant powers to act when safeguarding issues arise. However, there is an overall lack of proactivity across the different sectors. There are problems in relation to coercive control, self-neglect, financial abuse, corporate accountability, data sharing and independent advocacy. There is also little integration, cooperation, or data sharing across sectors.

The existing structures governing adult safeguarding are limited and siloed. They focus on Health and Social Care, rather than across the board. That is why the creation of a new standalone authority which prioritises inter-agency cooperation is essential.

The Law Reform Commission recommends effective interagency cooperation, which is currently absent from frontline safeguarding services and is hampering the safeguarding and protection of social workers. It also prevents HIQA, An Garda Síochána and other stakeholders from sharing information and working together to deal with cases of abuse and neglect of adults.
A useful starting point would be the creation of a Working Group on Adult Safeguarding, led by the Department of Health, working together with relevant

Departments and Agencies. The Working Group should be tasked with progressing adult safeguarding legislation and whole-of-government policy, and planning for the creation of a new adult safeguarding authority.

The Law Reform Commission also recommends that new legislation should include the introduction of a statutory requirement/duty to be placed on all relevant services for interagency working and information sharing when it is necessary within the context of protecting at-risk adults. Interim regulations, guidance documents and codes of practice should be developed to enable this.
The McIlroy Report outlines strong evidence for interagency collaboration being a key pillar of safeguarding practice.

All policy concerning adult safeguarding should prioritise collaboration. The introduction of a Memorandum of Understanding between the HSE, HIQA and An Garda Síochána would also be useful, focused on the identification and reporting of abuse and neglect of adults.

There should be training for all staff members involved in adult safeguarding so that they know who they can share information with and when. Safeguarding Ireland recommends that we have a public education and awareness programme on safeguarding. This would encourage inter-agency cooperation by clarifying the parameters for information sharing.
There should be a statutory obligation and permission for information sharing between all the different agencies where there is a concern around safeguarding.

The Department of Health should ensure the national collection of data across different sectors, which will incorporate a framework and statutory basis for interagency cooperation, collaboration, and data sharing.
Several groups should be involved in inter-agency cooperation, including the HSE, the
Department of Health, the Data Protection Commission, HIQA, the HSE’s National
Safeguarding Office and the National Independent Review Panel, the Policing and
Community Safety Authority, An Garda Síochána, the Decision Support Service, the
Central Bank of Ireland and the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman.
Independent Advocacy
Independent advocacy is an important resource for individuals who are at risk of abuse, yet advocacy supports have not been prioritised for funding and lack statutory independence and standing.

Independent advocacy plays an important role in supporting people to make and communicate decisions and participate in decisions about their own lives, including their finances, residency, support systems, neglect and abuse.

Independent advocacy means advocacy support provided by individuals or organisations that are independent of service providers and family members. It aims to assist and empower individuals who face obstacles in exercising their rights by ensuring that they can express their views, participate in decision-making, and communicate their wishes.

Currently, statutory duties to facilitate access to independent advocacy in safeguarding contexts are limited to adults with disabilities and older people residing in residential centres and people with mental health disorders receiving treatment in residential settings. A uniform approach has not been taken in these centres, therefore the strength of obligations placed on service providers varies significantly across the regulations.

Given that these obligations only apply to providers in certain settings, adults who are cared for outside of these centres do not have a statutory entitlement to access independent advocacy support. The Law Reform Commission recommends that the
Government should adopt a consistent approach to the provision of advocacy across all care settings.

Where a person’s liberty is restricted, they should have access to independent advocacy to ensure their will and preference is heard. Individuals need to know they have equal rights when issues of safeguarding arise and that they are not tied to somebody else. Independent advocates are organisations that are independent and can offer help.

The Law Reform Commission recommends that all organisations and individuals engaging with an at-risk person should abide by three principles – protection, prevention and proportionality. A Code of Practice for advocates should be developed, but it must be regulated with a defined education standard and training involved.

There is an importance in empowering people to protect themselves. We need support mechanisms and community and societal awareness. The best way to safeguard people is by enabling them to safeguard themselves. Part of that involves putting preventative measures in place.

There are three aspects to safeguarding – the best form of safeguarding is prevention and all that happens before. This is about empowering people to keep themselves safe. Then it is about looking at how we respond, and the clinical expertise and training needed to respond to the issues and concerns we have. Afterwards, it is about what we to do support people’s lives after they experience trauma and how we support that.

Sage Advocacy saw a 56% increase in demand for its services after the assisted decision-making laws were introduced. The number of cases grew from 1,975 in 2023 to 3,086 in 2024. Its Information Support Service also grew by 53% in a 12-month period from 5,928 queries in Q4 2023 to 9,062 at the end of 2024. The largest
number of calls last year related to issues concerning nursing homes, finances and assisted decision-making.

The absence of a standalone safeguarding authority and legislation further hampers the development of independent advocacy. There are serious limitations to safeguarding without the establishment of an independent authority and there needs to be legislative provision for independent advocacy. The authority should have responsibility for raising awareness among professionals and the public on using independent advocacy.
